axioms: A relation type is only real if it carries a checkable inverse/symmetry/domain-range definition; anything else is a label, not an ontology.

Contradiction detection is a property of declared axioms, not of the specific data seen so far — a validator that isn't derived from stated inverse/symmetry rules cannot generalize past the cases it was built against.
A classification scheme is only meaningful if it can express 'no good fit'; forced classification into the nearest bucket is silent data corruption, not coverage.
Two authoritative sources describing the same edge set require one explicit, stated tie-break rule; anything less is an unversioned race condition waiting on whoever edits next.
Derived structure (e.g. cycles, feedback loops) must be reproducible from a stated definition over a stated subgraph, not asserted as a bare count.
A schema must be able to grow (new types, new relations) without invalidating data already classified under the prior version, or the ontology cannot mature alongside its content.
failure_mode: Visual and perceptual legibility of the resulting graph (color, layout, label placement, density at render time) — this lens reasons about data correctness, not about how the data is drawn.
Runtime or performance cost of validation and derivation at scale.
Narrative, tone, or prose quality of descriptions and mechanics text.
User-facing workflow, interaction design, and information architecture of the surfaces that consume the data.
Organizational or scheduling feasibility of running two work tracks in parallel — it only catches structural collisions in the data model itself, not people/calendar collisions.
